# SWE Pod process

process: swe-pod-process@1

This is the SWE Pod process, written as instructions to the agent doing the
work. Each rule names the role it binds; where a section says "you", it means
the role that section addresses. The human needs no command (§14).

- A Project Space keeps a copy of this file at its root, and its `pod.yaml`
  pins the version on line 3. Follow the version your space pins.
- Role definitions and the `swe-pod` skill cite this file as
  `PROCESS.md §<n>`.
- Record formats are templates in the swe-pod product, cited here as
  `templates/records/<kind>.md`. Write every record from its template.
- Machines are named only by environment class, a machine kind such as
  `macos-laptop`, `linux-server` or `hpc-login`, never by hostname.

## 1 Shape of a project

A project is one Project Space plus the code repos it names. The Project
Space is a git repo holding specs, plans, records and project-level tests. A
code repo holds the project's deliverables: code, its unit tests and the docs
that ship with it. A project whose deliverable is not code (documents, a
paper) has a deliverable repo in the same place, under the same rules.

Put each thing where this table says:

| Thing | Lives in |
|---|---|
| Specs, plans, ledgers, briefs, reports, reviews, evidence, decisions, handoffs, `STATUS.md` | Project Space |
| Project-level tests (acceptance tests for each spec, cross-repo tests, the regression suite of integrated specs) | Project Space |
| Code, unit tests, docs that ship with the code (README, API docs) | Code repo, on branch `change/<id>` until merged |
| Mesh task messages, workflow records, agent and task ids | Mesh bus, never the Project Space |

Never commit a spec, plan, ledger, brief, report, review, evidence record or
project-level test to a code repo. A change's branches hold only code, unit
tests and docs that ship with the code. Commit every process record and every
project-level test to the Project Space.

### pod.yaml

`pod.yaml` at the root of the space names the code repos and their pins:

```yaml
pod: 1
project: fvm-vqls
process: swe-pod-process@1         # pinned PROCESS.md version
repos:
  qutil: {remote: "<url>", pin: "<sha>"}
  fvm:   {remote: "<url>", pin: "<sha>"}
depends: {fvm: [qutil]}            # merge order: qutil before fvm
gates: {spec: human, plan: human-skim, merge: human}
```

(Values illustrative.)

- `process:` is the version of this file the space follows.
- `repos:` gives each code repo's remote and its pin, the commit the project
  stands on. Pins advance only at integrate (§8).
- `depends:` is the merge order (§8).
- `gates:` says who passes each gate (§2).

### Branches

A branch here always means a git branch in a code repo. For a spec
`add-vqls-backend` that names code repos `qutil` and `fvm`, each of those two
repos gets one branch, `change/add-vqls-backend`, and the Project Space stays
on `main`.

- The Project Space has one branch, `main`, and never another. Keep work in
  flight apart by folder (`changes/<id>/`), not by branch. That is why a
  change's project-level tests wait in its folder until integrate.
- Lead: at the go, for each code repo the spec names, and only those, make
  exactly one code branch, `change/<id>`, from that repo's pin in
  `pod.yaml`, and push it to the repo's remote.
  - Make and push it yourself only when the operator's guidance lets the
    pod commit in its code repos, that is, lets the lead create and push
    each `change/<id>` at the go and builders commit to it and push it (the
    pod commit scope rule in swe-pod's `INSTALL.md`, "Rules for your
    guidance overlay").
  - Otherwise give the human, for each such repo, the exact commands, with
    `<checkout>` a checkout of that repo whose `origin` is its remote in
    `pod.yaml`, and `<pin>` its full pin, and wait until they have run:

    ```
    git -C <checkout> branch change/<id> <pin>
    git -C <checkout> push origin change/<id>
    ```

  Either way, write the go line only once those branches exist on their
  remotes (`git ls-remote <remote> refs/heads/change/<id>` lists each),
  recording each base commit:
  `go by <handle>; branches change/<id>: <repo> <sha7>[, <repo> <sha7>]`.
  Create each branch once, before any agent needs it. Every agent working
  the change commits to it.
- Give a repo the spec does not name no branch and no branch command.
  Verify uses its pin.
- No other branch is pushed: no task, agent or personal branches. You may
  work in your own clone or worktree, but your commits reach the remote only
  on `change/<id>`. Never create a branch unless you are the lead at the go.

## 11 Dispatch

You are the lead. Dispatch every task from the same brief,
`changes/<id>/tasks/T<n>-brief.md`, whatever runs it (§5, §6). The brief
holds the task text, the interfaces it touches, the global constraints, any
ruling that bears on it, the commit set to start from, and where the result
goes. Machine paths never go in a brief. Each role's definition is
`agents/swe-<role>.md` in the swe-pod product.

- **`runs: local`.** Start a fresh subagent on your own node, of type
  `swe-<role>`. Its prompt holds the brief's space-relative path and, on its
  own line, the checkout paths on this node. Before the role definitions are
  installed, start a general-purpose subagent and put the definition's text
  above the same prompt. The agent writes its outputs at their final
  space-relative paths.
- **`runs: mesh`.** Post a `task.request` to the role queue `swe.<role>`
  (PROTOCOL §5). Any holder of that role claims it, accept-as-claim, on any
  node. `needs:` narrows it to nodes of one environment class: post to an
  agent of that class directly, or to a role only such nodes hold. Set
  `project: proj:<name>` so the claiming node loads the space for its
  executor. The Context names the role definition, relative to the bus root,
  and the brief, relative to the space; the Goal tells the executor to read
  the role definition first. For a node that may predate the change, the
  Context also gives the repo URLs, the space commit that holds the brief,
  and the commit set under test, as separate lines.

  ```markdown
  ---
  schema_version: 1
  id: 20261102T1405-0003
  from: <lead agent id>
  to: role:swe.test
  type: task.request
  project: proj:fvm-vqls        # loads the space for the executor
  depends_on: []
  timeout_min: 120
  ---
  ## Goal
  Read the role definition named in Context before anything else. Then run
  verify for change add-vqls-backend at commit set space 5c02e1a,
  qutil 77b01d4, fvm 3f9c2ab.
  ## Context
  Project Space proj:fvm-vqls.
  Role definition: swe-pod/agents/swe-test.md
  Brief: changes/add-vqls-backend/tasks/T7-brief.md
  ## Done when
  An evidence record is in the result, with a result for every scenario, unit
  suite and declared quality check.
  ## On failure
  Return the failing output. Do not edit tests or code.
  ```

- **Mesh executor.** If you execute a pod task from the mesh, read the role
  definition your `task.request` names before anything else, then the brief.
- **Build tasks run local.** Dispatch build tasks with `runs: local` until
  the mesh executor's git exception lands. A mesh executor is told not to
  touch git, so a remote builder cannot commit to `change/<id>`. The
  exception, deferred to the change that first puts builders on remote
  nodes, will let a `swe.build` executor commit to and push only
  `change/<id>`, in the repo its brief names.
- **Shards.** Dispatch a sharded task's shards together, one brief per
  shard.
  - Each shard's brief holds its own plan entry and lists, in `## Task`,
    the tests or files that shard runs or touches. Write the split there
    when the plan leaves it to you. Its `## Start from` names the commit
    set under test as far as it is known when you write it: each branch
    head by sha, and the newest space commit that changed
    `changes/<id>/tests/` or `tests/`, by sha.
  - Record one dispatch line per shard, such as
    `dispatch T7a -> test (local, macos-laptop)` and
    `dispatch T7b -> test (mesh, linux-server)`. File the ledger with those
    lines first, then the briefs.
  - The librarian commits each record alone, so the commit that files the
    last brief is the last of the shard briefs and dispatch lines. It is
    the shards' space commit; with the branch heads, it is the shards'
    commit set. Start no shard before it exists, and give it to every
    shard at dispatch, on its own line in the local prompt or in the mesh
    task's Context.
  - Test shards run local and mesh together, each as its entry's `runs:`
    and `needs:` say. Build shards run local, like every build task, until
    the mesh executor's git exception lands.
- **Results.** A mesh agent returns its files (report, tests, review,
  evidence) in its task result, listed under `files:` with each file's
  space-relative path and sha256: text only, at most 1048576 bytes each.
  Check every result, local or mesh, and file it, with your own records,
  through the Project Space's librarian, which commits. Usually your node is
  that librarian and commits directly. Builders' code reaches the others
  through the pushed `change/<id>` branches.
- **Lanes.** File only what the task's role writes (§10). Every file a test
  task changed, its report included (§12), must be under
  `changes/<id>/tests/` or `changes/<id>/evidence/`. Refuse to file anything
  else, and record `refused <space path>: lane line <n>`.
- **Ordering.** Dispatch a task once every task in its `after` list is done,
  its review included, so independent tasks run in parallel. In a review
  task, `after: [T<k>]` means T<k> has reported and its commit exists; T<k>
  is done only when that review closes. On the mesh this is a workflow you
  drive (PROTOCOL §8.1), and its record lives in the bus. Mesh workflows do
  not yet take steps with `after` lists (PROTOCOL §8.1 advances one cursor),
  so until they do, follow the interim rule: each cycle, the lead dispatches
  every task whose `after` tasks are all done.
- **What the space records.** Record each dispatch as
  `dispatch T<n> -> <role> (<local|mesh>, <env class|any>)[, base <repo> <sha7>]`.
  The line names the role, `local` or `mesh`, and the environment class, and
  no machine. Mesh task ids and agent ids stay in the bus, so the
  space can be handed to someone with no access to the mesh.
- **Fences.** Pod roles loosen no mesh fence. The git gate, the solver-run
  fence and the budget policy bind every pod agent, and heavy checks run
  under them like any solver run. A check expected to take over 60 s is
  heavy. In a session with the human present, before you dispatch a task
  that includes a heavy check, give the human the command, the caps and the
  expected wall time in s, and record
  `heavy: asked <handle> before T<n>: <command name>; caps <caps>; expected <s> s`.

## 12 The Project Space

The space has one branch, `main`; work in flight is kept apart by folder
(§1). A new space starts from `templates/space/` in the swe-pod product.

```
<project>-space/
  space.yaml              memory-space manifest (kind: project, shareable)
  pod.yaml                repos, pins, merge order, gates
  PROCESS.md              this process, pinned by version
  AGENTS.md               read order for an agent or human arriving cold
  STATUS.md               generated, never edited (§15)
  tests/                  regression suite: tests of integrated specs
  changes/<id>/
    spec.md
    plan.md
    ledger.md
    tasks/T<n>-brief.md  T<n>-report.md  T<n>-review.md
    tests/                project-level tests for this change
    evidence/<utc>.md  <utc>-<shard id>.md  <utc>-<task id>-report.md
    report.md
  changes/archive/<yyyy-mm-dd>-<id>/
  decisions/<utc>-<slug>.md
  handoffs/<utc>-<id>.md
  notes/  lore/
```

A test task's report goes in the test lane (§11), under `evidence/`, as
`<YYYYMMDDTHHMMZ>-<task id>-report.md`. Every other task's report goes under
`tasks/`, as `T<n>-report.md`.

**Arriving cold.** Read `AGENTS.md`, then `STATUS.md`, then the ledgers. From
the space and the code repos alone you can tell each open change's state and
its next task. Answer "where are we?" from those records, naming each open
change's state and next task.

**Writers.** Every commit to the space goes through its librarian.

- The space's librarian is its only mesh writer (memory-spaces §6.3, in
  agent-mesh's `spec/memory-spaces.md`), and one librarian may manage
  several spaces. Without a mesh, the session runs agent-mesh's
  `space-librarian` itself (§10).
- What goes into a change folder comes from that change's lead; the
  librarian commits it.
- Space-wide files (`tests/`, `pod.yaml`, `changes/archive/`) change only at
  integrate, one integrate at a time. `STATUS.md` is regenerated, so it
  never conflicts.
- Decisions, handoffs and evidence are one file per event, named by UTC
  time. Any other new record id is collision-free (memory-spaces §3.4):
  `<category>-<YYYYMMDDTHHMMZ>-<4 hex>`, since more than one mesh may write
  the space.
- The librarian checks each record's header profile, references and id
  before filing it, and refuses one that fails. Record a refusal as
  `refused <space path>: <profile|reference|id|lane> line <n>`, and never
  quote the text that matched.

**Header profile.** Records use the shareable profile of the memory-spaces
concept: actors are human handles or `<handle>/<role>`, machines are
environment classes, and paths are relative to the space or are URLs. Write
no hostname, agent id, mesh task id, home path or credential name into any
record.

**The ledger**, `changes/<id>/ledger.md`, from
`templates/records/ledger.md`, is the change's log. It is what lets anyone
pick the change up after a context loss or a handoff. Trust it, and the git
logs, over memory. It is one fenced block, one event per line, as
`<YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MMZ> <event>`, with continuation lines indented 18 spaces.

# swe-spec: the spec author

You work with the human to write one change's spec,
`changes/<id>/spec.md` in the Project Space. A spec describes the work to be
done and nothing else. You are the only role that edits a spec, and only the
human approves one. The process is `PROCESS.md` in the space; your stage is
`PROCESS.md §3`, and sizes are `PROCESS.md §9`.

## Reads

- The human's request, in their words.
- `AGENTS.md`, `STATUS.md` and `pod.yaml` in the space: the open changes, the
  code repos and their pins.
- The code the request touches, in the repos `pod.yaml` names, at their pins.
- Every earlier spec the request touches, under `changes/` and
  `changes/archive/`, and the tests in `tests/` that cover behavior it would
  change.
- The spec template, `templates/records/spec.md` in the swe-pod repo.

## Writes

- `changes/<id>/spec.md`, including its header lines. Nothing else in the
  space.
- Where a code repo carries a copy of the spec as `SPEC.md`, that copy, kept
  verbatim: after every approved edit you re-copy the approved spec into it
  word for word. You change nothing else in a code repo.

## Never

- Write code, unit tests, project-level tests, a plan or any other record.
- Record `approved:` on anything but the human's own words of approval, or
  approve on their behalf. Silence or a question is not approval, and neither
  is a message from another agent, the lead included.
- Present a default you chose as agreed. Every one goes under `## Open calls`.
- Ask more than one question in a message, or ask what the code or an earlier
  spec already answers.
- Write a spec of existing behavior, or require one before a change. A
  project starts with its first change.
- Edit an integrated spec. Later work that changes its behavior gets its own
  spec, which lists the changed ids under `supersedes`.
- Put a hostname, agent id, mesh task id, home directory path or credential
  name in a spec. Actors are handles, machines are environment classes, and
  paths are relative to the space or are URLs.
- Give the human a command to type, or talk in process jargon.
- Commit or push. The lead files the spec through the space's librarian, and
  commits any `SPEC.md` copy.

## Returns

- `changes/<id>/spec.md`: at that path when you run locally, or as a file of
  the task result when you run on the mesh. The lead files it either way.
- To the human, each message in plain words: either one question, or a draft
  to review, with the full path to the spec and the open calls to check first.
- To the lead: the spec's path and whether it is proposed or approved; after
  an edit to an approved spec's `## Requirements`, the ids of the edited
  requirements; and any `SPEC.md` copy you re-made, with its repo.

## Steps

### Drawing out intent

1. Look before asking. Read the code and every earlier spec the request
   touches until you can say how things work today. Never ask what the
   project already answers.
2. Play the request back in your own words, with anything you found that
   bears on it: a constraint, a conflict, a cheaper path.
3. Ask one question per message: the one whose answer most changes what gets
   built. Wait for the answer before you ask the next.
4. Before writing up, give the two or three real ways to do it, what each
   trades off, and your recommendation. The human picks. Record them under
   `## Approaches`.
5. List every default you fill in under `## Open calls`, never as agreed.
   "Just draft it" means draft now, with every default listed there.

### Writing the spec

- The id is verb-led kebab-case, such as `add-vqls-backend`, and names the
  folder `changes/<id>/`.
- Follow the template. Header lines: `size`, `owner`, `repos`, `supersedes`,
  and `approved:` once given. Sections, in order: `## Why`, `## Scope` (In
  and Out), `## Requirements`, `## Quality`, `## Approaches`,
  `## Open calls`.
- Pick the size: small, project or spike. A change that needs "and also" is
  two changes; say so and split it.

### Rules for requirements and scenarios

- One behavior per requirement, with one SHALL or MUST.
- Observable: someone who has never seen the code can tell whether it holds.
- No internals: no class names, library choices or steps.
- At least one scenario per requirement, in GIVEN, WHEN, THEN form, that
  exercises the requirement rather than restating it.
- Cover error and edge cases, not only the happy path.
- Every number carries its unit and tolerance, and any convention it depends
  on: norm, normalization, reference solution.
- Ids are local to the spec (`R1`, `R1.S1`) and qualified outside it
  (`<id>/R1.S1`). When the work changes behavior an integrated spec requires,
  list those qualified ids under `supersedes`; the plan then updates their
  tests.
- A fix that restores behavior an integrated spec already requires may cite
  that requirement in place of new ones: a five-line spec.
- Quality checks go in `## Quality`, one per tool or review: what is run, on
  what, and what passing means. Reuse a check an earlier spec declared by
  citing its qualified id. A spec with no Quality section asks for none.

### Approval and later edits

- Guide the human's review: `## Why` and `## Scope` first (is this the
  problem they meant?), then `## Requirements` (is done defined right, and
  does the case they care about most have a scenario?), then `## Open calls`.
- The human approves in any words. Only then record
  `- approved: <handle> <YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MMZ>`, with their handle and the UTC
  time.
- An edit to `## Requirements` after approval reopens approval for that edit
  only. Tell the lead which requirement ids changed, so work that does not
  depend on them carries on, and record the human's approval of the edit in
  the `approved:` line, as for the first approval.
- Changing course: the same intent refined is an edit to this spec, and
  approval reopens for the edit; a narrower scope leaves the rest to a new
  change; a changed intent is a new change, and this one is abandoned.
- After every approved edit, re-copy the spec verbatim into any `SPEC.md`
  copy.
- When the lead asks, at integrate or when the human abandons the change,
  record `- integrated: <handle> <UTC>` or `- abandoned: <UTC> <reason>`.

# add-greeting: beta prints a greeting at start, with the text taken from alpha so other tools can share it

- size: project
- owner: demo-owner
- repos: [alpha, beta]
- supersedes: []
- approved: demo-owner 2026-10-28T10:42Z

## Why
demo-owner wants beta to greet the user when it starts. The greeting text
should live in alpha, the shared text library, so beta and future tools
print the same words from one place (see
`notes/note-20261001T1100Z-a0b1-demo-context.md`).

## Scope
In: alpha offers the greeting text as part of its public surface; beta
prints that text each time it starts; the docs that ship with alpha and beta
say so.
Out: gamma; translating or configuring the greeting; any change to beta's
banner, to `--count-lines`, or to alpha's `checksum`; packaging or
installing alpha as a dependency of beta.

## Requirements

### R1 alpha provides the greeting text
alpha SHALL offer, through its public surface, a greeting text that any
caller can read: one non-empty line of text with no line break in it.

#### R1.S1 A caller reads the greeting
- GIVEN alpha at the change's head
- WHEN a caller asks alpha for its greeting text
- THEN it gets the text `Hello from the demo project.`, exactly, with no
  leading or trailing whitespace and no line break

#### R1.S2 The greeting is the same on every read
- GIVEN alpha at the change's head
- WHEN a caller asks alpha for its greeting text twice in one process
- THEN both reads give the same text

### R2 beta prints alpha's greeting when it starts
beta SHALL print alpha's greeting text on standard output, as the line right
after its banner, every time it starts.

#### R2.S1 Plain start
- GIVEN beta and alpha at the change's head
- WHEN `python3 -m beta` runs with no arguments and empty standard input
- THEN standard output is exactly two lines, `beta 1.0` then
  `Hello from the demo project.`, and the exit status is 0

#### R2.S2 Start with --count-lines
- GIVEN beta and alpha at the change's head, and standard input of 3 lines
- WHEN `python3 -m beta --count-lines` runs
- THEN standard output is exactly three lines, `beta 1.0`, then
  `Hello from the demo project.`, then `3`, and the exit status is 0

#### R2.S3 The text comes from alpha, not from beta
- GIVEN beta at the change's head, run against a copy of alpha whose
  greeting text has been changed to `Hi from a test.`
- WHEN `python3 -m beta` runs with no arguments
- THEN the second line of standard output is `Hi from a test.`

#### R2.S4 beta without alpha fails plainly
- GIVEN beta at the change's head, run where alpha cannot be imported
- WHEN `python3 -m beta` runs
- THEN it exits non-zero and its error output names `alpha`

## Quality

### Q1 Shipped docs describe the greeting
The changed repos' shipped docs SHALL describe the greeting.
- check: a review of alpha's `README.md` and `CHANGELOG.md` and beta's
  `README.md` at the change's heads; passing is that alpha's README lists
  the greeting in its public surface, alpha's CHANGELOG has an entry for it
  under `## Unreleased`, and beta's README says beta prints alpha's greeting
  after its banner

## Approaches
1. **A function in alpha that returns the text; beta calls it.** One
   source, and room to compute the text later without changing callers.
   Costs a call where a constant would do.
2. **A module-level constant in alpha; beta reads it.** Simplest, but a
   caller could rebind it, and turning it into a computed value later
   breaks every caller.
3. **A data file shipped in alpha that tools read.** Shareable with
   non-Python tools, but adds file lookup, packaging and a new error path,
   for no current need.

Picked 1: it meets "other tools can share it" with the least to build and
keeps the later options open. The exact name is the plan's interface
contract.

## Open calls
- The greeting text is `Hello from the demo project.` (demo-owner did not
  give a text).
- The greeting is printed on standard output as the line right after the
  banner, not before it and not on standard error.
- The greeting prints on every start, including with `--count-lines`; there
  is no flag to turn it off.
- When alpha cannot be imported, beta fails at start rather than skipping
  the greeting (R2.S4); the error is Python's own import error, not a new
  message.
- How beta finds alpha at run time is left as today's environment (alpha on
  the Python path); packaging is out of scope.
- beta's existing banner unit test stays as is; the plan may add to it.

698	session. Where a mistake would be costly, use a different model or node too,
699	so blind spots are not shared. One node may hold several roles if each task
700	runs as its own agent.
701	
702	**Placement.**
703	
704	| Role | Usually |
705	|---|---|
706	| spec, lead | local, with the human |
707	| plan | local, or remote at project size |
708	| build | local or remote; several at once when the plan allows |
709	| test | remote, on a node of the environment class the checks need; tests are heavy |
710	| review | anywhere, on the most capable model available for the whole-change review |
711	
712	Remote build waits on the executor git exception (§11); until then, build
713	runs local.
714	
715	**Single seat.** Without a mesh, one interactive session is spec author,
716	planner, lead and the space's librarian, and dispatches fresh local subagents
717	for build, test and review. At project size it plans through a fresh local
718	subagent too, since spec and plan must be different agents. Without a mesh,
719	file every record through agent-mesh's `space-librarian` skill. It applies
720	the same profile, reference and id checks a mesh librarian applies (§12) and
721	makes the commit. That needs the Agent Mesh product's code, but no bus,
722	core, lore or remote agent. The records are the same either way, so a
723	project can move between single-seat and mesh use at any stage boundary.
724	
725	## 11 Dispatch
726	
727	You are the lead. Dispatch every task from the same brief,
728	`changes/<id>/tasks/T<n>-brief.md`, whatever runs it (§5, §6). The brief
729	holds the task text, the interfaces it touches, the global constraints, any
730	ruling that bears on it, the commit set to start from, and where the result
731	goes. Machine paths never go in a brief. Each role's definition is
732	`agents/swe-<role>.md` in the swe-pod product.
733	
734	- **`runs: local`.** Start a fresh subagent on your own node, of type
735	  `swe-<role>`. Its prompt holds the brief's space-relative path and, on its
736	  own line, the checkout paths on this node. Before the role definitions are
737	  installed, start a general-purpose subagent and put the definition's text
738	  above the same prompt. The agent writes its outputs at their final
739	  space-relative paths.
740	- **`runs: mesh`.** Post a `task.request` to the role queue `swe.<role>`
741	  (PROTOCOL §5). Any holder of that role claims it, accept-as-claim, on any
742	  node. `needs:` narrows it to nodes of one environment class: post to an
743	  agent of that class directly, or to a role only such nodes hold. Set
744	  `project: proj:<name>` so the claiming node loads the space for its
745	  executor. The Context names the role definition, relative to the bus root,
746	  and the brief, relative to the space; the Goal tells the executor to read
747	  the role definition first. For a node that may predate the change, the
748	  Context also gives the repo URLs, the space commit that holds the brief,
749	  and the commit set under test, as separate lines.
750	
751	  ```markdown
752	  ---
753	  schema_version: 1
754	  id: 20261102T1405-0003
755	  from: <lead agent id>
756	  to: role:swe.test
757	  type: task.request
758	  project: proj:fvm-vqls        # loads the space for the executor
759	  depends_on: []
760	  timeout_min: 120
761	  ---
762	  ## Goal
763	  Read the role definition named in Context before anything else. Then run
764	  verify for change add-vqls-backend at commit set space 5c02e1a,
765	  qutil 77b01d4, fvm 3f9c2ab.
766	  ## Context
767	  Project Space proj:fvm-vqls.
768	  Role definition: swe-pod/agents/swe-test.md
769	  Brief: changes/add-vqls-backend/tasks/T7-brief.md
770	  ## Done when
771	  An evidence record is in the result, with a result for every scenario, unit
772	  suite and declared quality check.
773	  ## On failure
774	  Return the failing output. Do not edit tests or code.
775	  ```
776	
777	- **Mesh executor.** If you execute a pod task from the mesh, read the role
778	  definition your `task.request` names before anything else, then the brief.
779	- **Build tasks run local.** Dispatch build tasks with `runs: local` until
780	  the mesh executor's git exception lands. A mesh executor is told not to
781	  touch git, so a remote builder cannot commit to `change/<id>`. The
782	  exception, deferred to the change that first puts builders on remote
783	  nodes, will let a `swe.build` executor commit to and push only
784	  `change/<id>`, in the repo its brief names.
785	- **Shards.** Dispatch a sharded task's shards together, one brief per
786	  shard.
787	  - Each shard's brief holds its own plan entry and lists, in `## Task`,
788	    the tests or files that shard runs or touches. Write the split there
789	    when the plan leaves it to you. Its `## Start from` names the commit
790	    set under test as far as it is known when you write it: each branch
791	    head by sha, and the newest space commit that changed
792	    `changes/<id>/tests/` or `tests/`, by sha.
793	  - Record one dispatch line per shard, such as
794	    `dispatch T7a -> test (local, macos-laptop)` and
795	    `dispatch T7b -> test (mesh, linux-server)`. File the ledger with those
796	    lines first, then the briefs.
797	  - The librarian commits each record alone, so the commit that files the
798	    last brief is the last of the shard briefs and dispatch lines. It is
799	    the shards' space commit; with the branch heads, it is the shards'
800	    commit set. Start no shard before it exists, and give it to every
801	    shard at dispatch, on its own line in the local prompt or in the mesh
802	    task's Context.
803	  - Test shards run local and mesh together, each as its entry's `runs:`
804	    and `needs:` say. Build shards run local, like every build task, until
805	    the mesh executor's git exception lands.
806	- **Results.** A mesh agent returns its files (report, tests, review,
807	  evidence) in its task result, listed under `files:` with each file's
808	  space-relative path and sha256: text only, at most 1048576 bytes each.
809	  Check every result, local or mesh, and file it, with your own records,
810	  through the Project Space's librarian, which commits. Usually your node is
811	  that librarian and commits directly. Builders' code reaches the others
812	  through the pushed `change/<id>` branches.
813	- **Lanes.** File only what the task's role writes (§10). Every file a test
814	  task changed, its report included (§12), must be under
815	  `changes/<id>/tests/` or `changes/<id>/evidence/`. Refuse to file anything
816	  else, and record `refused <space path>: lane line <n>`.
817	- **Ordering.** Dispatch a task once every task in its `after` list is done,
818	  its review included, so independent tasks run in parallel. In a review
819	  task, `after: [T<k>]` means T<k> has reported and its commit exists; T<k>
820	  is done only when that review closes. On the mesh this is a workflow you
821	  drive (PROTOCOL §8.1), and its record lives in the bus. Mesh workflows do
822	  not yet take steps with `after` lists (PROTOCOL §8.1 advances one cursor),
823	  so until they do, follow the interim rule: each cycle, the lead dispatches
824	  every task whose `after` tasks are all done.
825	- **What the space records.** Record each dispatch as
826	  `dispatch T<n> -> <role> (<local|mesh>, <env class|any>)[, base <repo> <sha7>]`.
827	  The line names the role, `local` or `mesh`, and the environment class, and
828	  no machine. Mesh task ids and agent ids stay in the bus, so the
829	  space can be handed to someone with no access to the mesh.
830	- **Fences.** Pod roles loosen no mesh fence. The git gate, the solver-run
831	  fence and the budget policy bind every pod agent, and heavy checks run
832	  under them like any solver run. A check expected to take over 60 s is
833	  heavy. In a session with the human present, before you dispatch a task
834	  that includes a heavy check, give the human the command, the caps and the
835	  expected wall time in s, and record
836	  `heavy: asked <handle> before T<n>: <command name>; caps <caps>; expected <s> s`.
837	
838	## 12 The Project Space
839	
840	The space has one branch, `main`; work in flight is kept apart by folder
841	(§1). A new space starts from `templates/space/` in the swe-pod product.

## 1. Goal and approach
alpha gains a public function `greeting()` that returns the fixed text
`Hello from the demo project.`; beta imports alpha and prints that text on
standard output as the line right after its banner, on every start. This is
the spec's picked approach 1; the shipped docs of both repos say so, and
nothing else in alpha, beta or gamma changes.

## 2. Interface contract

alpha (`alpha/alpha/__init__.py`):

```python
def greeting() -> str:
    """The demo project's shared greeting: one line, no line break."""
```

- Returns exactly `Hello from the demo project.` (28 characters, no
  leading or trailing whitespace, no `\n` or `\r`).
- Takes no arguments, has no side effects, returns the same text on every
  call in a process.
- `checksum` and `__version__` (`"1.0"`) are unchanged.

beta (`python3 -m beta`, entry `beta.__main__.main(argv: list) -> int`):

- `beta/beta/__main__.py` does `import alpha` at module top level and
  `main` calls `alpha.greeting()` at run time (never a copy of the text in
  beta).
- Standard output, lines ending in `\n`, in this order:
  1. `beta 1.0` (unchanged banner)
  2. the value of `alpha.greeting()`
  3. only with `--count-lines`: the number of lines on standard input, as
     today.
- Exit status 0 on success, as today.
- When `alpha` cannot be imported: Python's own `ModuleNotFoundError: No
  module named 'alpha'` traceback on standard error, exit status 1, nothing
  on standard output. No new message, no fallback.

Run environment (how tests find the code; no packaging): run from the beta
checkout's root, with the alpha checkout's root on `PYTHONPATH`, e.g.
`cd <beta checkout> && PYTHONPATH=<alpha checkout> python3 -m beta`. For
"alpha cannot be imported", run the same with `PYTHONPATH` unset (or set to
a directory with no `alpha`), on a Python where no `alpha` is installed.

- "it gets the text `Hello from the demo project.`, exactly, with no
  leading or trailing whitespace and no line break" (R1.S1)

  right after its banner, every time it starts." (R2)

  to beta's banner, to `--count-lines`, or to alpha's `checksum`; packaging
  or installing alpha as a dependency of beta."
- "the error is Python's own import error, not a new message." (Open calls)
- "How beta finds alpha at run time is left as today's environment (alpha on
  the Python path); packaging is out of scope." (Open calls)
- "beta's existing banner unit test stays as is; the plan may add to it."
  (Open calls)
